Newborn Common bent-wing bats (Miniopterus schreibersii) enter the world as altricial neonates, completely dependent upon maternal care. At the moment of parturition, these pups weigh approximately 2.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.8 grams], a remarkably modest mass given the species' ultimate adult size. This initial body mass, measured directly from neonates in a maternity roost, represents a critical starting point for the rapid growth phase that follows. The gestation period that precedes this live birth is a carefully timed affair, lasting 100 days [tg = 100 days] under the stable, warm conditions of a maternity cave maintained at a body temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]. This relatively extended gestation, compared to other insectivorous bats of similar size, is thought to allow for significant organogenesis in utero. Following birth, the altricial pups are unable to thermoregulate effectively and rely on clustering with their mothers and other females to maintain their core temperature. The energetic investment required for this initial mass is substantial, setting the stage for the subsequent developmental milestones that will lead to independent flight and foraging.

The suckling juvenile stage is characterized by intense parental investment and a steep growth trajectory, culminating in complete nutritional independence. At this point of weaning, the young bat has reached a body mass of about 12.5 grams [Wwx = about 12.5 grams], representing a nearly five-fold increase from its birth weight. This wet weight at weaning is a strong indicator of the quality of maternal provisioning and the availability of insect prey in the surrounding habitat. Juveniles that achieve a higher mass at this critical juncture tend to exhibit better survival rates during their first winter. The cessation of milk feeding marks a profound shift in the juvenile's ecology, as it must now navigate the complex three-dimensional world of aerial insectivory entirely on its own.

Sexual maturation in the Common bent-wing bat exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in its timing, a common pattern among polygynous mammals. Under the stable thermoregulatory conditions of a bat at rest, often maintained at 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C], females reach the onset of puberty and become capable of reproduction at roughly 577 days after birth [tp = roughly 577 days after birth]. This critical life-history transition is marked by the first ovulation and the development of the reproductive tract. In contrast, males require a longer developmental period to achieve full reproductive viability, typically attaining sexual maturity at approximately 730 days after birth [tp = approximately 730 days after birth] at a temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]. This disparity is frequently attributed to the intense intrasexual competition among males for access to females during the mating season, which places a premium on larger body size and greater experience. Delayed male maturation ensures that by the time a male begins competing for mates, he has accrued the physical size and behavioral skills necessary to secure a territory or a position within a male-dominated roost hierarchy.

The ultimate adult body size and maximum recorded longevity of this species reflect a life-history strategy oriented toward relatively slow development and extended survival. The maximum recorded body mass for a healthy, reproductively active adult is roughly 13 grams [Wwi = roughly 13 grams], a figure derived from extensive trapping studies across multiple colonies. This ultimate wet weight is characteristic of a bat that has completed all somatic growth and is fully invested in reproduction or maintenance. Longevity data from banding studies are particularly impressive for such a small mammal. The maximum lifespan observed in wild populations, recorded from individuals banded as juveniles and recovered years later, is approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years] at a body temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]. This extraordinary lifespan is roughly double that recorded for some similar-sized mammals, a difference profoundly shaped by the species' hibernation habits, which dramatically reduce metabolic rates for a significant portion of the year. A field study tracking one individual over two decades revealed that it was still actively lactating at 20 years of age, underscoring the species' remarkable reproductive and somatic persistence.

The annual reproductive schedule is also remarkably conservative, with females producing just one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], meaning the maximum daily reproduction rate for this species is effectively limited to a single offspring annually. This low fecundity is offset by the exceptionally high adult survival rates afforded by the species' longevity and the safety of their communal roosting sites. In comparative terms, the reproductive rate of a single pup per year is significantly lower than that of many other insectivorous mammals of similar body mass, but it is entirely consistent with a slow-paced, "bet-hedging" life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high reproductive output in a variable environment.
